Learning Objectives
Perform an appropriate evaluation and workup of patients with a forearm fracture, especially
with regard to emergent clinical scenarios (eg, compartment syndrome).
Identify fracture patterns and associated surgical or nonsurgical management.
Describe anatomy and risks associated with forearm approaches for the surgical fixation of
forearm fractures.
Identify signs and symptoms of postoperative complications.
Describe treatment strategies for postoperative complications.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy

Overview
Most diaphyseal forearm fractures in adults are managed surgically. Outcomes of nonsurgical
management of most diaphyseal forearm fractures in adults are inferior to those of surgical
management. The exception is isolated diaphyseal ulna fractures with limited displacement
and angulation.
The best report of closed management indicates a loss of more than 50° of rotation in 30% of
patients.
Plate and screw fixation techniques resulted in decreased rates of nonunion and malunion
and better functional outcomes compared with intramedullary fixation.
Management of diaphyseal fractures of the forearm in adults via open reduction and plate and
screw fixation is considered the standard against which all other treatment options currently
are compared.
Epidemiology
The incidence of forearm shaft fractures in adults is 1.35 per 10,000 individuals.
Common etiologies include falls at home (30%), motor vehicle collisions (14%), and sports
injuries (14%).
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
The axis of rotation for pronation/supination of the forearm extends from the center of the
radial head through the ulnar styloid and is independent of elbow position.
The radial bow accommodates pronation of the forearm.
The bow is not purely in the sagittal or coronal plane.
The mean maximum radial bow in the coronal plane is approximately 15 mm and is located
60% distally along the axis of the radius (Figure 1).

Figure 1 Illustration shows measurement of the location and magnitude of the maximum
radial bow in the coronal plane. The maximum bow measures a mean 15 mm (a) and 60%
distal along the length of the radius (x/y × 100). (Reproduced with permission from
Schemitsch EH, Richards RR: The effect of malunion on functional outcome after plate
fixation of fractures of both bones of the forearm in adults. J Bone Joint Surg Am
1992;74[7]:1068-1078.)
Straightening of the radius may contribute to loss of rotation and grip strength.
Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand questionnaire scores correlated with pronation in
a study in which researchers evaluated patients at a mean follow-up of 34 months after both-
bone forearm fracture surgery; however, no correlation existed between motion and
Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand questionnaire scores in two studies with longer
evaluation periods.1-3
The ulna also is bowed.4,5
An ulnar bow distributed along the distal 75% of the bone and occurs in sagittal and coronal
planes; and the apex is consistently distal to the radial bow.
A mean of 5.7° of proximal ulna dorsal angulation also is present. Surgeons should be aware
of this angulation during surgical fixation, especially in patients with a metadiaphyseal
fracture pattern.
Vascular Anatomy

The radial and ulnar arteries branch from the brachial artery 1 cm distal to the elbow joint at
the level of the radial neck.
The radial artery is adherent to the deep fascia of the flexor carpi radialis longus, at which it is
encountered during the Henry exposure of the radius.
Most gunshot fractures in civilians result from low-velocity pistols, which are uncommonly
associated with vascular injury or neurotmesis. Most nerve palsies associated with low-velocity
gunshot fractures will recover spontaneously. The nerves may be explored during open
reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) to confirm they are intact.
Neural Anatomy
The median nerve runs with the brachial artery and passes between the two heads of the
pronator teres deep to the biceps aponeurosis and superficial to the brachialis. The nerve then
runs between the flexor digitorum superficialis and the flexor digitorum profundus before
entering the carpal tunnel.
Proximally, the anterior interosseous nerve separates from the median nerve to innervate the
flexor pollicis longus and the index and long flexor digitorum profundus and terminates in the
pronator quadratus.
The ulnar nerve enters the forearm between the two heads of the flexor carpi ulnaris and
courses along the forearm to innervate the ring and little flexor digitorum profundus and
terminates distally as palmar and dorsal sensory branches.
The radial nerve, at the level of the forearm, is separated into a superficial and a motor
branch. The superficial branch is adherent to the deep fascia of the brachioradialis, at which it
is encountered during exposure of the radius according to the interval described by Henry.
The deep branch of the radial nerve (also known as the posterior interosseous nerve [PIN])
courses dorsally around the radial neck to pierce the supinator and runs along the posterior
interosseous membrane and the floor of the fourth dorsal wrist compartment, terminating
within the wrist capsule.
Tendons
The biceps insertion onto the radius is an important landmark for proximal exposure of the
radius through the interval described by Henry. Just adjacent to this is the bicipital tuberosity
and then, continuing radially, the supinator muscle through which the PIN runs.

The pronator teres inserts onto the mid-radius. For fractures in the middle and distal one-
third, it can be left in place, with the plate applied directly on top. Alternatively, it can be
elevated subperiosteally. It may be easier to preserve this insertion if the plate is placed on the
direct radial surface of the radius.
The wrist flexor and extensor muscles and the extrinsic muscles for the digits have muscle
bellies in the proximal and mid-forearm. Distally, these transition to tendons.
The palmaris longus is superficial, is not present in all patients, and should not be mistaken for
the median nerve, which is a deeper structure.
The flexor carpi radialis is an important superficial structure because it is the primary tendon
identified via the volar approach to the distal radius.
The flexor carpi ulnaris and the extensor carpi ulnaris form the interval between which the
ulna is exposed.
The contents of the carpal tunnel comprise the flexor digitorum superficialis, the flexor
digitorum profundus, and the flexor pollicis longus, as well as the median nerve.
At the wrist, the extensor tendons lie within compartments.
The first dorsal compartment contains the abductor pollicis longus and the
extensor pollicis brevis tendons.
The second dorsal compartment contains the extensor carpi radialis brevis and longus
tendons.
The third dorsal compartment contains the extensor pollicis longus tendon.
The fourth dorsal compartment contains the extensor indicis proprius and the extensor
digitorum communis tendons.
The fifth dorsal compartment contains the extensor digiti minimi tendon.
The sixth dorsal compartment contains the extensor carpi ulnaris tendon.
Joints and Ligaments
Surgeons should consider the forearm as a single articular unit composed of the proximal and
distal radioulnar joints and stabilized by the annular ligament, the interosseous ligament
(including its distal oblique band), and the distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ) ligament.
The interosseous ligament connects the ulna to the radius obliquely, 21° proximal to the
transverse axis of the forearm (Figure 2).
Axial load is transmitted from the distal radius to the proximal ulna via the interosseous
ligament.

The proportion of axial load is estimated to be 80% radius at the wrist, with an increasing
amount of load borne proximally by the ulna, depending on elbow position.
The central fibers are on maximal tension in neutral rotation.
The distal fibers are on maximal tension in supination.
Figure 2 Illustrations of forearms show the relationship between the radius, ulna, and
interosseous membrane (IOM). The orientation of the IOM transfers axial load from the distal
radius to the proximal ulna. The axis of rotation of the forearm extends from the center of the
radial head to the ulnar styloid. DRUJ = distal radioulnar joint, MRUJ = middle radioulnar joint,
PRUJ = proximal radioulnar joint. (Reproduced from McAndrew CM: Forearm trauma and
diaphyseal fractures, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3.
Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 953-960.)
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury

Diaphyseal forearm injuries typically are associated with high-energy trauma, such
as motorcycle crashes, motor vehicle collisions, or falls from a height.
Assault with a blunt object (ie, ulnar nightstick fractures) and penetrating injuries
(ie, gunshot wounds) also are common causes of these injuries.
Low-energy fractures may occur in patients with osteoporosis or pathologic fracture related to
malignancy.
Special Consideration: Compartment Syndrome of the Forearm
Associations or etiological factors include high-energy fracture, crush injury, spontaneous
hematoma, constrictive dressings, and revascularization
After fixation of a diaphyseal fracture of the forearm, the fascia is not closed to limit the
potential for compartment syndrome.
The keys to diagnosis are clinical pain with passive stretch of the forearm muscles and
disproportionate pain.
Distraction because of severe pain from other injuries, altered mentation, or neurologic injury
may make these symptoms unreliable.
Nerve dysfunction is a later finding. Loss of sensation (including subtle findings such as loss of
threshold sensibility) usually precedes motor dysfunction.
Compartment pressures higher than 30 mm Hg that persist for more than 8 hours may be
associated with irreversible muscle and nerve damage.
A pressure gradient of less than 30 mm Hg between compartment pressure and diastolic
blood pressure may be an indication for fasciotomy.
The incidence of acute compartment syndrome associated with diaphyseal fractures of the
forearm is approximately 3.1%.
Because the forearm compartments are interconnected, release of the superficial volar
compartment is thought to be adequate unless extensive crush injury is present. The carpal
tunnel should be released (Figure 3).

Figure 3 Dorsal and volar illustrations of forearms show the skin incisions for forearm
fasciotomy. Adequate volar fasciotomy includes mobile wad fasciotomy, lacertus fibrosus
release, volar extrinsic muscle fasciotomy, and carpal tunnel release. Dorsal compartment
pressures often decrease with volar fasciotomy. (Reproduced from McAndrew CM: Forearm
trauma and diaphyseal fractures, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review,
ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 953-960.)
Separate release of the mobile wad fascia, the lacertus fibrosus, the extensor compartment,
and the deep volar compartment fascia is not thought to be routinely necessary. If concern
exists that compartment syndrome will persist without release of these areas, compartment
pressures can be remeasured intraoperatively.
The flexor digitorum profundus and the flexor pollicis longus (the deepest volar muscles)
typically are affected most severely in patients with Volkmann ischemic contracture.

Special Consideration: Compartment Syndrome of the Forearm
The clinician should be vigilant for compartment syndrome in patients with a high-
energy forearm fracture.6,7 Type C fractures and gunshot fractures of the proximal one-
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:10 PM
AAOS | Forearm Trauma and Diaphyseal Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001169
8/36

third are associated with compartment syndrome.8 Any clinical suspicion of a
compartment syndrome should warrant decompression and fasciotomy. Intra-
compartment pressure measurements may be useful in patients who are obtunded or
intubated. Given that most fractures of the radius and ulna in the diaphysis are managed
surgically, the compartments generally are released with exposure of the bones. If
concern for compartment syndrome exists, a longer proximal extension can be made to
ensure the entire volar compartment is released and release of the carpal tunnel may be
considered. If wound closure is tight, the wounds should be left open, with skin grafting
or closure performed after swelling has decreased sufficiently.
Injury Classification
Isolated Radial Shaft Fracture
Defined as a radial shaft fracture with no DRUJ dislocation and less than 5 mm of ulnar positive
variance on injury radiographs (Figure 4)
Epidemiology—Approximately three-fourths of radial shaft fractures without associated ulnar
shaft fracture have less than 5 mm of ulnar positive variance on injury radiographs.
Anatomy—Most in the middle one-third of the radius
Fractures in the proximal one-third may be associated with dislocation of the proximal
radioulnar joint (PRUJ); this may not be apparent on initial radiographs of the elbow.9
Surgical approaches—The volar (Henry) approach is preferred by most surgeons for all
diaphyseal radius fractures. The dorsal (Thompson) approach in the proximal forearm is
associated with greater risk to the PIN, particularly if the plate is removed.
Radiographic evaluation—Includes orthogonal radiographs that include the wrist, forearm,
and elbow; if no subluxation or dislocation of the DRUJ or PRUJ is present and ulnar variance is
less than 5 mm, the diagnosis is an isolated radial shaft fracture.
Management and rehabilitation—ORIF; restoring the relationship of the radius and ulna is
followed by early (less than 2 weeks) active range of motion (ROM) and no weight bearing until
the fracture heals.
Complications—Reported complications relate to iatrogenic nerve palsy (of the PIN), injury of
the superficial radial nerve, unappreciated PRUJ or DRUJ dislocation, infection, and nonunion.

Galeazzi Fracture
A radial shaft fracture associated with a DRUJ dislocation (Figure 5)

(Reproduced from Atesok KI, Jupiter JB, Weiss AP: Galeazzi fracture. J Am Acad Orthop Surg
2011;19[10]:623-633.)
With or without ulnar styloid fracture
Epidemiology—Approximately one-fourth of radial shaft fractures without an ulnar shaft
fracture are associated with DRUJ dislocation.
Anatomy—More than one-half of radial shaft fractures with an associated DRUJ dislocation
occur in the distal one-third.

Surgical approaches
A volar (Henry) approach is used for internal fixation of the radius fracture.
Fixation may be considered for an associated ulnar styloid base fracture. A longitudinal
approach over the extensor carpi ulnaris tendon sheath is used, with protection of the
superficial transverse ulnar nerve branches.
Mechanism of injury—Fall on an outstretched hand
Management
If the DRUJ cannot be reduced, then exploration to remove interposed soft tissues (most
commonly the extensor carpi ulnaris, extensor digiti minimi, or extensor digitorum
communis) is considered.10
DRUJ usually is stable after anatomic plate-and-screw fixation of the radius.
If the DRUJ dislocates with forearm motion, evaluate alignment of the radius. In addition,
assess for plastic deformation of the ulna, particularly in patients younger than 25 years. If
instability is not related to these factors and a stable position of the forearm can be
identified (usually supination), then immobilization of the forearm in that position for
approximately 4 weeks is considered. If the forearm is unstable in all positions, then trans-
fixation of the ulna to the radius with the use of two Kirschner wires and immobilization for 4
weeks are considered. An ulnar styloid base fracture may be present in patients with
instability; however, fixation of the fracture alone may not restore stability because the distal
radioulnar ligaments may not be attached to it and may be associated with dorsal ulnar
nerve irritation and hardware problems.
Rehabilitation—After ORIF of the radius, motion is encouraged after a brief period of
immobilization for comfort. No forceful use or weight bearing is recommended until fracture
healing is confirmed. Immobilization in a splint or cast or via pin fixation for 4 to 6 weeks is
reserved only for an unstable DRUJ, with active ROM initiated immediately after splint or pin
removal.
Complications
Usually related to undiagnosed associated injuries to the elbow or a missed DRUJ injury
Long-term follow-up demonstrates equivalent subjective and objective outcomes in patients
with and without DRUJ dislocation at the time of injury if treated appropriately; however,
considerable disability may result in patients not treated appropriately.11
Monteggia Fracture
A fracture of the proximal one-third of the ulna, with associated radial head dislocation from
the PRUJ (Figure 6).

Figure 6 AP (A) and lateral (B) elbow radiographs demonstrate a Bado type II Monteggia
fracture with posterior angulation of the ulna and posterior dislocation of the radial head.
(Reproduced from Ring D, Jupiter JB and Waters PM: Monteggia fractures in children and
adults. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 1998;6[4]:215-224.)
Epidemiology
Uncommon in adults
More common in children, with peak incidence occurring between ages of 4 and 10 years
Anatomy—Energy from the ulnar fracture travels through the interosseous membrane,
eventually leading to rupture of the annular ligament and disruption of the proximal
radioulnar and radiocapitellar joints.
Surgical approaches
Approach to ulna: midline posterior incision with proximal deep interval between the flexor
carpi ulnaris and the anconeus and the distal deep interval between the flexor carpi ulnaris
and the extensor carpi ulnaris
Approach to radial head (very uncommonly used): most often via the Kaplan approach, with
the deep interval between the extensor carpi ulnaris and the extensor digitorum communis
Mechanism of injury—Direct blow to the forearm with the elbow in extension and the forearm
in hyperpronation
Bado classification system (Figure 7)

Figure 7 Illustrations show the Bado classification of Monteggia fractures, which is
determined by the direction in which the radial head dislocates. Type I, anterior. Type II,
posterior. Type III, lateral. Type IV, associated radiocapitellar dislocation in any direction.
(Reproduced from Kim JM, London DA: Complex Monteggia fractures in the adult cohort: Injury
and management. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2020;28[19]:e839-e848.)
Type I: ulnar fracture with apex anterior angulation and anterior dislocation of the radial
head
Type II: ulnar fracture with apex posterior angulation and posterior dislocation of the radial
head
Type III: ulnar fracture with apex lateral angulation and lateral dislocation of the radial head
Type IV: fracture of proximal one-third of the ulna and radius, with dislocation of the radial
head in any direction

Jupiter classification of posterior Monteggia fractures (Figure 8)
Figure 8 Illustrations show the Jupiter subtypes of Bado type II Monteggia fractures. Type IIA
includes distal olecranon and coronoid process fractures. Type IIB includes a proximal ulna
fracture distal to the coronoid process at the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction. Type IIC is a
pure diaphyseal ulna fracture. Type IID is a comminuted ulna fracture extending from the
trochlear notch to the metaphysis with inclusion of the coronoid. (Reproduced from Kim JM,
London DA: Complex Monteggia fractures in the adult cohort: Injury and management. J Am
Acad Orthop Surg 2020;28[19]:e839-e848.)
Type II A: fracture of the ulna involving the distal olecranon and the coronoid process
Type II B: fracture at the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction, distal to the coronoid process
Type II C: ulnar fracture in the diaphysis
Type II D: fracture extends to the proximal one-half of the ulna
Management
Plate-and-screw fixation of the ulnar fracture, which almost always results in closed
reduction of the radial head; preferred in adults
If the radial head does not reduce, then the proximal ulna most likely is malreduced; in many
patients, proximal ulna dorsal angulation has not been restored.
Rehabilitation

Brief immobilization (less than 2 weeks) for comfort, then active, self-assisted stretching
exercises
With posterior Monteggia lesions, surgeons should consider elbow motion with an overhead
motion protocol to reduce the risk of subluxation or dislocation.
No restrictions if the fracture is healed, approximately 4 months postoperatively
Complications
Mostly observed in patients with a Bado type II fracture and include radioulnar synostosis
and posterolateral rotatory instability12
PIN palsies may be observed in patients with anterolateral PRUJ dislocation.
Isolated Ulnar Shaft Fracture ( Nightstick Fractures)
Natural healing with brace or cast support; associated with high union rates and good
function without surgical treatment in most patients.
Anatomy—Most fractures occur in the middle one-third of the ulna.
Surgical approach—Direct approach to the subcutaneous border between the flexor
carpi ulnaris and extensor carpi ulnaris
Mechanism of injury
Usually a direct blow to the ulnar forearm (defensive position)
May result from rotational stress
These injuries (identified during the history taking) should alert the clinician to the
possibility of associated elbow pathology.
Clinical evaluation
The distal neurovascular status, the soft-tissue envelope, and pain at the elbow and wrist
should be evaluated.
Evaluation of the PRUJ to exclude injury is paramount.
Radiographic evaluation
Includes radiographs of the wrist, forearm, and elbow
Displacement of more than 50% of the shaft width and angulation of more than 10° have
been associated with alteration of forearm rotation, leading to consideration of surgical
management (Figure 9).

ulnar shaft fracture. (Reproduced from Rosenwasser MP, Zeltser DW: Fractures of the
forearm and distal radius, in Ricci WM, Ostrum RF, ed: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update:
Trauma, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2016, pp 309-
336.)
Management
Nonsurgical management with short-term (2 weeks) immobilization, followed by active ROM
is recommended for fractures with no evidence of wrist, elbow, or interosseous instability.
Surgical management may be considered for fractures with more than 10° of angulation
and/or greater than 50% shaft-width displacement.
Rehabilitation
Patients who elect to undergo nonsurgical treatment often are allowed to move immediately
in a wrist or forearm brace.
Active motion is encouraged postoperatively.
Complications

If associated elbow injury is excluded, complication rates are low.
Nonunion occurs in approximately 10% of patients treated nonsurgically, and appropriate
patient/injury selection can reduce this rate.13 (Figure 10)
Figure 10 Radiographs of the forearm of a patient with an isolated ulnar shaft fracture.
Preoperative AP (A) and lateral (B) views demonstrate an isolated ulnar shaft fracture. The
patient was treated via splint immobilization, went on to nonunion, and required surgical
repair 6 months postinjury. AP (C) and lateral (D) views obtained 4 weeks postoperatively
demonstrate increased consolidation at the fracture site and well-positioned hardware.
(Courtesy of Jaclyn Jankowski, DO, Jersey City, NJ.)
Coulibaly et al14 found a 12% nonunion rate in patients treated nonsurgically (compared with
5.4% in patients treated surgically).
The authors also found that female sex, increased age, and noncompliance with weight-
bearing restrictions were associated with an increased risk of nonunion.14
Both-Bone Forearm Fractures
Mechanism of injury
High energy transfer required to fracture the diaphyseal section of both bones of the
forearm; commonly results from motor vehicle collisions and falls from a height onto the
upper extremities, with bending moments and direct blows causing the fractures.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:10 PM
AAOS | Forearm Trauma and Diaphyseal Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001169
19/36

Low-energy injuries with resulting fractures should alert the clinician to possible associated
elbow and wrist pathology.
Clinical evaluation
Should include distal neurovascular examination, soft-tissue envelope evaluation, and
exclusion of compartment syndrome
A thorough patient history includes handedness and employment/hobby expectations.
Radiographic evaluation
Includes orthogonal radiographs of the wrist, forearm, and elbow
Contralateral radiographs may assist the treating surgeon by providing a template for
reconstruction.
Management
Surgical management is recommended for both-bone forearm fractures in patients older
than 10 years if the patient is able to tolerate surgery (Figure 11).
Figure 11 Preoperative (A) and postoperative (B) lateral forearm radiographs demonstrate
a both-bone forearm fracture. (Reproduced from McAndrew CM: Forearm trauma and
diaphyseal fractures, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3.
Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 953-960.)
Longitudinal Radioulnar Dissociation (Essex-Lopresti Lesion)15

9/3/26, 4:10 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001169

Most commonly associated with radial head fracture, which allows for proximal migration if
excision or inadequate reconstruction is performed
Proximal migration of the radius results in relative ulnar positivity of the ulna distally, limiting
forearm supination and wrist extension (Figure 12).
Figure 12 Illustration of the forearm shows proximal migration of the radius, which can
occur secondary to a comminuted radial head fracture and damage of the interosseous
membrane and also is known as an Essex-Lopresti lesion. (Reproduced from Rozental TD,
Beredjiklian PK, Bozentka DJ: Longitudinal radioulnar dissociation. J Am Acad Orthop Surg
2003;11[1]:68-73.)
Recognition of the acute injury and management are paramount for optimal function because
late reconstruction procedures result in limited success.
Restoration of radial length via anatomic reduction or reconstruction/arthroplasty is the first
step to successful management.
Stabilization of the DRUJ in supination, possibly via pin fixation, is performed if necessary.

Mechanics of Fractures

Mechanics of Fractures
Fractures may result from several etiologies. Direct blows secondary to trauma
typically result in short oblique or transverse fractures isolated to the radius or the ulna.
Falls onto an outstretched hand cause axial load, which may result in torsional and axial
forces that may lead to not only fractures in the radius and/or ulna but also associated
ligamentous injuries (ie, Essex-Lopresti or Galeazzi fractures). Same-level fracture
patterns about the radius and ulna typically indicate high-energy injuries. Penetrating
trauma (eg, gunshot wounds) may result in blast fractures, which are associate with a
high rate of nondisplaced fracture extension, which often is not visible on plain
radiographs.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
A comprehensive patient history, including the mechanism of injury, is important to not only
confirm diagnosis but also rule out associated injuries. High-energy injuries should alert the
clinician to potential compartment syndrome.
Physical Examination
The clinician should assess the overall appearance of the forearm, including the presence of
any open fractures. Overall swelling also should be observed and monitored. Concurrent
ligamentous injury of the DRUJ or the interosseous membrane may be present in patients who
report pain at those specific anatomic areas and should be examined accordingly. Suspected
instability always can be compared with an intact contralateral extremity.
Neurovascular Examination
Proper neurovascular status always should be established at baseline. Motor and sensory
examination of the radial, ulnar, and median nerve distributions always should be established.

Concern for compartment syndrome, pain with passive stretch, and/or any motor or sensory
changes should increase suspicion. In addition, an Allen test should be performed to establish
vascular dominance of the injury; this may be performed in the operating room if the patient is
too uncomfortable on initial evaluation.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
AP and lateral radiographs that afford visualization of the forearm from the wrist to the elbow
If doubt exists with regard to the alignment of the DRUJ or PRUJ, specific wrist and elbow
radiographs can be obtained.
Computed Tomography
CT may be helpful in the rare instance in which a radiographically occult fracture is possible
and would alter management.
CT may aid in the evaluation for potential intra-articular extension that may affect surgical
planning.
In patients with a fragmented fracture, particularly those caused by gunshot wounds, CT may
help delineate the extent of the fracture, which may extend more distally or proximally than
that observed on radiographs, allowing for selection of proper plate length intraoperatively.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI may be helpful in patients in whom interosseous ligament injury is suspected; however, its
reliability and accuracy are unknown.16
Ultrasonography
In adult patients, ultrasonography has limited applications.
In pediatric patients, ultrasonography is comparable to fluoroscopy (with less radiation) in
visualizing alignment after reduction.17

Other than isolated ulnar shaft fractures, a limited role exists for nonsurgical treatment in
adults with a diaphyseal forearm fracture.
Indications
Isolated ulnar shaft fractures
Patients who are too infirm to undergo surgical fixation
Surgical Management
Indications
All both-bone forearm fractures should be managed surgically.
Contraindications
Patients who are too infirm to undergo surgical fixation should be treated nonsurgically.
Techniques/Procedures
Preoperative Planning
Contralateral radiographs may aid in proper restoration of the anatomic bow of the radius and
the ulna.
Associated management of the DRUJ (splinting versus pinning); contralateral extremity
examination may help determine laxity.
Templating for lag screw and neutralization versus bridge plating
Patient Positioning
Supine on a hand table
To approach the ulna, the extremity can be flexed at the elbow.
Surgical Approaches18
The volar approach to the radius (Henry approach) is commonly used (Figure 13).

The skin incision is longitudinal from lateral to the biceps tendon to the radial styloid, with the
length dictated by the necessary exposure of the radius.

ligated to allow for ulnar retraction.

retracted radially with the muscle.

Proximally, the radius is exposed lateral/radial to the biceps insertion (the radial artery is
medial/ulnar to the tendon).
With the forearm in full supination, the insertion of the supinator muscle is identified and
released.
Subperiosteal dissection from ulnar to radial protects the PIN within the supinator muscle.
In the middle one-third of the forearm, slight pronation exposes the insertion of the pronator
teres muscle. Subperiosteal release of the pronator teres from radial to ulnar exposes the
radial shaft.
Distally, the pronator quadratus and the flexor pollicis longus are released from their radial
origins ulnarly, exposing the distal radius. Distally, the superficial radial nerve lies between the
brachioradialis and the extensor carpi radialis longus tendons, becoming superficial 9 cm
proximal to the radial styloid.

Fracture or osteotomy reduces the effect of forearm pronation, and the PIN is found closer
to the radiocapitellar joint in these situations.
The abductor pollicis longus and the extensor pollicis brevis can be retracted distally (middle
one-third) or proximally (distal one-third) to expose the radius.
Exposure of the ulna is performed along the subcutaneous border.
The interval between the extensor carpi ulnaris (PIN) and the flexor carpi ulnaris (ulnar nerve)
is used.
The ulnar nerve and artery are volar to the flexor carpi ulnaris muscle and are at risk if this
muscle is not carefully dissected directly off the ulna.
The dorsal cutaneous branch of the ulnar nerve extends from the ulnar nerve 6.4 cm from the
distal end of the ulna and becomes subcutaneous 5.0 cm from the proximal edge of the
pisiform.
Surgical Techniques
ORIF with interfragmentary compression is the preferred treatment option and the standard
against which other approaches are compared.2
Interfragmentary screw application with neutralization plating is appropriate for spiral and
oblique fractures.
Compression plating with (oblique; Figure 16) or without (transverse) interfragmentary screw
compression through the plate also can be used.

If the fracture is comminuted such that interfragmentary compression is not feasible, a

rotation, is used (Figure 17). Contralateral radiographs of the uninjured elbow, forearm, and
wrist are used as a template.

Most commonly, the radius is fixed with the use of a 3.5-mm plate or a stiff, 2.7-mm locking
compression plate if the bone is small. More flexible reconstruction plates should be avoided.
Intramedullary fixation has been studied in small case series and can result in comparable union
rates and ROM.20
The ulna is fixed antegrade, with an entry point in the olecranon process.
The radius is fixed retrograde, with an entry point just ulnar to the Lister tubercle.
Temporary external fixation may be used in emergent situations or if soft-tissue compromise
prevents safe ORIF. Safe half-pin fixation can be applied through the subcutaneous border of the
ulna and the dorsal/radial border of the radius, with blunt dissection and retraction to protect
soft-tissue structures.

Standard dressings can be used without splinting to promote early ROM and function.
The wrist can be splinted for a short time for comfort.
For Galeazzi fractures, splinting in the stable position can be performed for 2 weeks, after
which ROM is permitted.
Pitfalls and Preventive Measures
For radius fractures and both-bone fractures, appropriate fixation to allow for active motion
should be achieved.
Staged closure, with possible later skin grafting, may be helpful if a risk of compartment
syndrome or muscle necrosis exists.
Likely radiographic union should be documented before unrestricted activity is permitted,
usually after 4 months.
Complications
Splints and casts should be checked frequently to avoid pressure ulcers and skin injury.
Infection should always be ruled out as a cause of any nonunion, hardware failure, and/or
persistent pain.
Nonunion
May occur in as many as 5% of patients who undergo compression plating
Risk factors for nonunion include extensive comminution, inadequate fixation, and infection.
Management
Hypertrophic nonunions require appropriate application or reapplication of balanced
fixation.
Atrophic nonunions can be managed via repeat plating and autologous bone grafting
(cancellous or corticocancellous).21 In patients with a septic atrophic nonunion, an induced-
membrane technique can be used.22,23
Malunion
Incomplete restoration of the radial bow and residual angulation of the ulna may restrict
forearm rotation and decrease grip strength.

May occur postinjury or after surgical fixation
Close monitoring is important, especially for both-bone forearm and high-energy fractures.
Staged closure with or without skin grafting may be required for both-bone forearm fixation.
Rehabilitation
Barring severe comminution, segmental bone loss, concomitant injuries to the extremity, or
severe soft-tissue injury, the goal of surgical fixation is to provide enough stability to allow for
immediate functional ROM of the elbow, forearm, and wrist.
Weight bearing is limited until bone healing has progressed to tolerate loads (6 to 8 weeks).
DRUJ instability may require immobilization, with or without pin stabilization, for 4 to 6 weeks
after ORIF.
Outcomes
Mild losses in active ROM in pronation (7° less than normal), supination (9° less than normal),
wrist flexion (11° less than normal), and wrist extension (5° less than normal) are expected
after surgical fixation of both-bone forearm fractures via plate fixation that involves no
complications.
Reduced strength in pronation (70% of normal), supination (68% of normal), wrist flexion (84%
of normal), wrist extension (63% of normal), and grip (75% of normal) are expected after
uncomplicated surgical management of both-bone forearm fractures via plate fixation.
Good subjective results (mean Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand questionnaire
scores ranging from 12 to 18) can be achieved overall; however, poorer outcomes are
associated with decreased ROM, strength, and pain.
Pearls and Pitfalls
Evaluate for compartment syndrome and potential ligament injury.
Standard fixation involves the use of 3.5-mm plates and screws, resulting in with high union
rates.
Functional outcomes are directly correlated with proper restoration of anatomic radial
bow/length.
